title: Propositional Logic
explanation: Propositional logic deals with statements that are true or false and combines them with operators: AND, OR, NOT, IMPLIES, BICONDITIONAL.
analogy: Like boolean conditions in code. 'if (isAdmin AND isLoggedIn)' is a propositional formula. Each part is true or false, combined by operators.
tiny_visual_key: truth table with T/F values and logical operator symbols
example: P: 'It rains', Q: 'I take umbrella'. P → Q means 'If it rains, I take umbrella'. ¬P means 'It doesn't rain'.
why_it_matters: Propositional logic is the foundation of all programming conditions, circuit design, and formal verification. It's how we express and combine conditions.
checkpoint_question: When is P → Q (P implies Q) false?
expected_answer: Only when P is true and Q is false. If it rains (P true) but you don't take an umbrella (Q false), the implication is violated. All other combinations make it true.
common_mistake: Thinking implication works both ways. P → Q doesn't mean Q → P. 'If it rains, I take umbrella' doesn't mean 'If I take umbrella, it rains'.
key_insight: Implication P → Q is equivalent to ¬P ∨ Q. Either P is false (no promise to keep) or Q is true (promise kept).

title: Predicate Logic
explanation: Predicate logic extends propositional logic with quantifiers (∀ 'for all', ∃ 'exists') and predicates (statements with variables) to express relationships over domains.
analogy: Like programming with variables and loops. '∀x P(x)' is like 'for all x in domain, P(x) is true'. '∃x P(x)' is 'there exists some x where P(x) is true'.
tiny_visual_key: domain circle with universal/existential arrows over elements
example: ∀x (Student(x) → HasID(x)): All students have IDs. ∃x (Prime(x) ∧ Even(x)): Some prime is even (true: 2).
why_it_matters: Predicate logic lets us express properties of data structures, database queries, and program specifications. SQL WHERE clauses are predicate logic.
checkpoint_question: What's the negation of ∀x P(x)?
expected_answer: ∃x ¬P(x). If it's NOT true that all x satisfy P, then there EXISTS some x that doesn't satisfy P. Universal and existential swap when negated.
common_mistake: Confusing scope. In ∀x ∃y P(x,y), the y can be different for each x. In ∃y ∀x P(x,y), the same y must work for all x.
key_insight: Quantifier order matters. '∀x ∃y Loves(x,y)' (everyone loves someone) differs from '∃y ∀x Loves(x,y)' (someone is loved by all).

title: Logical Equivalences
explanation: Logical equivalences are formulas that always have the same truth value. They allow transforming complex expressions into simpler or more useful forms.
analogy: Like algebraic identities (a + b = b + a). You can rearrange logical formulas while preserving meaning, just as you simplify algebraic expressions.
tiny_visual_key: formula transforming through equivalent steps
example: De Morgan's: ¬(P ∧ Q) ≡ ¬P ∨ ¬Q. Double negation: ¬¬P ≡ P. Contrapositive: P → Q ≡ ¬Q → ¬P.
why_it_matters: Equivalences let you simplify circuit designs, optimize queries, prove theorems, and understand why conditions work the same different ways.
checkpoint_question: Why is the contrapositive of P → Q logically equivalent to P → Q?
expected_answer: Both are false only when P is true and Q is false. The contrapositive ¬Q → ¬P says 'if Q is false, P must be false' - the same constraint expressed differently.
common_mistake: Confusing contrapositive (equivalent) with converse (not equivalent). P → Q ≡ ¬Q → ¬P, but P → Q ≢ Q → P.
key_insight: De Morgan's laws are your most-used equivalences: flip the operator, negate the parts. !(A && B) = !A || !B.

title: Sets and Operations
explanation: A set is an unordered collection of distinct elements. Operations include union (∪), intersection (∩), difference (−), and complement (ᶜ).
analogy: Like groups of people. Union = everyone from either group. Intersection = people in both groups. Difference = people in one group but not the other.
tiny_visual_key: Venn diagrams showing set operations
why_it_matters: Sets model collections in programming (Set data structure), databases (UNION, INTERSECT), and are foundational to all discrete math.
checkpoint_question: What's the cardinality of A ∪ B given |A|, |B|, and |A ∩ B|?
expected_answer: |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| - |A ∩ B|. You add both sizes but subtract the intersection because it was counted twice.
common_mistake: Treating sets like lists. Sets have no order and no duplicates. {1,2,3} = {3,1,2} and {1,1,2} = {1,2}.
key_insight: Set operations parallel logical operations: union↔OR, intersection↔AND, complement↔NOT. Venn diagrams show both.

title: Functions and Relations
explanation: A function maps each input to exactly one output. A relation is a set of ordered pairs - functions are special relations with the uniqueness constraint.
analogy: A function is like a vending machine: put in a code, get exactly one item. A relation is like 'knows': a person can know many people or none.
tiny_visual_key: arrows from domain to range, function with single arrows per input
example: Function f(x) = x²: each x maps to one y. Relation 'divides': (2,4), (2,6), (3,6) - 2 maps to multiple values.
why_it_matters: Functions are everywhere in programming. Understanding injective, surjective, and bijective functions helps with reasoning about mappings and invertibility.
checkpoint_question: What makes a function bijective?
expected_answer: It's both injective (one-to-one: different inputs give different outputs) and surjective (onto: every output is reached by some input). Bijections have inverses.
common_mistake: Thinking all mappings are functions. If one input can give multiple outputs, it's a relation, not a function.
key_insight: A bijection pairs up domain and codomain perfectly. It proves two sets have the same size, even for infinite sets.

title: Permutations and Combinations
explanation: Permutations count ordered arrangements: n! ways to arrange n items. Combinations count unordered selections: C(n,k) ways to choose k items from n.
analogy: Permutation: arranging 3 books on a shelf (order matters). Combination: choosing 3 books to take on vacation (order doesn't matter).
tiny_visual_key: ordered arrangements vs unordered groups
example: Permutation: 3! = 6 ways to arrange ABC. Combination: C(5,2) = 10 ways to choose 2 items from 5.
why_it_matters: Counting problems appear in algorithms (how many paths?), probability, and combinatorics. Permutations and combinations are the foundation.
checkpoint_question: Why is C(n,k) = n! / (k!(n-k)!)?
expected_answer: There are n!/((n-k)!) ways to arrange k items from n. But we overcounted by k! since order doesn't matter in combinations, so divide by k!.
common_mistake: Using permutation when order doesn't matter. Choosing a committee of 3 is C(n,3), not P(n,3). Does swapping members create a 'different' result?
key_insight: Ask: does order matter? Yes → permutation. No → combination. This determines whether to divide by k!.

title: Pigeonhole Principle
explanation: If you put n+1 pigeons into n holes, at least one hole contains 2+ pigeons. More generally, if n items go into k bins, some bin has at least ⌈n/k⌉ items.
analogy: Like birthday paradox setup: if 367 people are in a room, at least 2 share a birthday - there are only 366 possible days.
tiny_visual_key: more items than containers, arrows showing collision
example: In any group of 13 people, at least 2 were born in the same month (12 months, 13 people).
why_it_matters: Pigeonhole proves existence without construction - you know something must exist even without finding it. Used in hash collision proofs and compression limits.
checkpoint_question: How many people are needed to guarantee 3 share a birth month?
expected_answer: 25 people. By generalized pigeonhole, we need (3-1)*12 + 1 = 25. With 24, you could have exactly 2 per month.
common_mistake: Forgetting +1. With n holes, n pigeons might fill them perfectly. You need n+1 to guarantee a collision.
key_insight: Pigeonhole proves impossibilities: you can't compress all files (more files than compressed representations), you can't avoid hash collisions with too many items.

title: Inclusion-Exclusion
explanation: To count elements in a union, add individual sizes, subtract pairwise intersections, add back triple intersections, and continue alternating.
analogy: Like counting attendees at overlapping events. Add all event counts, subtract people counted twice (at 2 events), add back people subtracted too much (at 3 events).
tiny_visual_key: Venn diagram with overlapping regions being added/subtracted
why_it_matters: Inclusion-exclusion solves 'how many satisfy at least one condition' problems, common in probability, counting, and algorithms.
checkpoint_question: Why do we alternate adding and subtracting in inclusion-exclusion?
expected_answer: Each level corrects the previous overcounting. Adding singles overcounts pairs. Subtracting pairs underounts triples. We oscillate to converge on the exact count.
common_mistake: Stopping too early. For n sets, you need all 2^n - 1 terms (all non-empty intersections). Missing terms gives wrong answers.
key_insight: Inclusion-exclusion for probability: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A ∩ B). Same principle, different domain.

title: Basic Probability
explanation: Probability measures likelihood on a 0-1 scale. P(A) = favorable outcomes / total outcomes for uniform distributions. Probabilities of all outcomes sum to 1.
analogy: Like fair dice. Each face has probability 1/6. The probability of rolling even (2,4,6) is 3/6 = 1/2.
tiny_visual_key: sample space divided into event region, ratio shown
example: Fair coin: P(heads) = 1/2. Die: P(prime) = P({2,3,5}) = 3/6 = 1/2.
why_it_matters: Probability underlies randomized algorithms, machine learning, data analysis, and understanding uncertainty in any system.
checkpoint_question: Why must P(A) + P(not A) = 1?
expected_answer: A and not-A together cover all outcomes (they're complements). Total probability is 1, and it's divided between A happening and A not happening.
common_mistake: Adding probabilities of non-mutually-exclusive events. P(A or B) ≠ P(A) + P(B) unless A and B can't both happen.
key_insight: P(not A) = 1 - P(A) is often easier to compute. Instead of counting successes, count failures and subtract.

title: Conditional Probability
explanation: P(A|B) is the probability of A given that B occurred. It's P(A and B) / P(B) - we restrict to the world where B happened.
analogy: Like asking 'what's the chance of rain tomorrow?' vs 'what's the chance of rain given clouds today?' Additional information changes the probability.
tiny_visual_key: sample space shrinking to B, probability recalculated in smaller space
why_it_matters: Conditional probability is how we update beliefs with new evidence. It's the foundation of Bayesian reasoning and many ML algorithms.
checkpoint_question: What's the difference between P(A|B) and P(B|A)?
expected_answer: They're generally different! P(rain|clouds) ≠ P(clouds|rain). P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B), P(B|A) = P(A∩B)/P(A). Different denominators.
common_mistake: The prosecutor's fallacy: confusing P(evidence|innocent) with P(innocent|evidence). These can be vastly different!
key_insight: Conditional probability 'shrinks' the sample space to events where B occurred. All recalculations happen within that smaller space.

title: Bayes' Theorem
explanation: Bayes' theorem relates P(A|B) to P(B|A): P(A|B) = P(B|A)·P(A) / P(B). It lets you flip conditional probabilities using prior beliefs.
analogy: Like a medical test. You know P(positive|disease) (sensitivity). Bayes tells you P(disease|positive) - what you actually want to know.
tiny_visual_key: prior flowing through likelihood to posterior
example: Test is 99% accurate, disease affects 1%. P(disease|positive) = (.99·.01) / P(positive) ≈ 50%, not 99%!
why_it_matters: Bayes' theorem is the foundation of Bayesian statistics, spam filters, medical diagnosis, and any system that updates beliefs with evidence.
checkpoint_question: Why can a 99% accurate test for a rare disease give mostly false positives?
expected_answer: Base rate matters. If disease is 1%, 99% of 1% true positives = 0.99%, but 1% of 99% false positives = 0.99%. About half of positives are false.
common_mistake: Ignoring base rates (the prior). High test accuracy doesn't mean high confidence in results if the condition is rare.
key_insight: P(A|B) = P(B|A)·P(A)/P(B). The prior P(A) matters enormously. Evidence updates beliefs, doesn't create them from nothing.

title: Expected Value
explanation: Expected value is the probability-weighted average of all possible outcomes. E[X] = Σ x·P(X=x). It's the long-run average if you repeat the experiment.
analogy: Like average game winnings. If you win $10 with 30% probability and $0 with 70%, expected value is $3 per game - your long-term average.
tiny_visual_key: outcomes weighted by their probabilities, summed
why_it_matters: Expected value guides decision-making under uncertainty. Comparing expected values helps choose between risky options rationally.
checkpoint_question: Can expected value be a value that never actually occurs?
expected_answer: Yes! Die expected value is 3.5, but you never roll 3.5. Expected value is an average over many trials, not a possible single outcome.
common_mistake: Thinking expected value guarantees anything in a single trial. It's a long-run average - short runs can deviate wildly.
key_insight: Linearity of expectation: E[X+Y] = E[X] + E[Y], even if X and Y aren't independent. This simplifies complex calculations enormously.

title: Graph Basics
explanation: A graph is vertices (nodes) connected by edges. Graphs can be directed (edges have direction) or undirected. They model relationships, networks, and connections.
analogy: Like a map of cities (vertices) and roads (edges). Directed graphs are like one-way streets. Undirected graphs are two-way roads.
tiny_visual_key: nodes as circles, edges as lines connecting them
example: Social network: people are vertices, friendships are edges. Web: pages are vertices, links are directed edges.
why_it_matters: Graphs model countless CS problems: networks, dependencies, routes, relationships. Graph algorithms are among the most important in CS.
checkpoint_question: What's the maximum number of edges in a simple undirected graph with n vertices?
expected_answer: n(n-1)/2 = C(n,2). Each pair of vertices can have at most one edge. This is the complete graph Kn.
common_mistake: Confusing vertices and edges in problem statements. 'Remove a node' means removing its edges too. 'Remove an edge' keeps the nodes.
key_insight: Choose representation based on density: adjacency matrix for dense graphs (O(1) edge check), adjacency list for sparse (O(V+E) space).

title: Graph Properties
explanation: Key properties: degree (edges per vertex), paths (sequences of edges), cycles (paths that return to start), connectivity (can reach all vertices).
analogy: Like analyzing road networks. Degree = roads from a city. Path = route between cities. Cycle = round trip. Connected = can drive anywhere.
tiny_visual_key: graph with labeled degrees, highlighted path and cycle
example: In directed graphs: in-degree (incoming edges) and out-degree (outgoing). Sum of all degrees = 2 × number of edges.
why_it_matters: Graph properties determine which algorithms apply. Cycles affect topological sort possibility. Connectivity determines reachability.
checkpoint_question: Why must the sum of all vertex degrees equal twice the edge count?
expected_answer: Each edge contributes 1 to the degree of both its endpoints. So counting degree sums counts each edge twice.
common_mistake: Forgetting that directed graphs have separate in-degree and out-degree. Paths in directed graphs must follow edge direction.
key_insight: If a graph has a vertex of degree 0, it's disconnected. If all degrees are at least 1, the graph may still be disconnected (multiple components).

title: Trees
explanation: A tree is a connected acyclic graph. It has n vertices and n-1 edges. Any two vertices are connected by exactly one path. Adding any edge creates a cycle.
analogy: Like a family tree or organizational hierarchy. No loops, one path between any two people, and removing any connection disconnects branches.
tiny_visual_key: tree structure with root, branches, no cycles
example: File system directories form a tree. DOM is a tree. Parse trees in compilers. Binary trees for search.
why_it_matters: Trees are the most common data structure in CS. They enable efficient search, parsing, hierarchical data, and divide-and-conquer algorithms.
checkpoint_question: Why does a tree with n vertices always have exactly n-1 edges?
expected_answer: Each vertex except the root has exactly one parent edge. That's n-1 edges. Fewer edges = disconnected, more edges = cycle.
common_mistake: Confusing tree properties with general graphs. In a tree, there's exactly one path between nodes - no need to search for shortest.
key_insight: Removing any edge disconnects a tree. Adding any edge creates exactly one cycle. Trees are 'minimal connected graphs'.

title: Proof Techniques
explanation: Common techniques: direct proof (assume P, derive Q), proof by contradiction (assume ¬Q, derive contradiction), proof by contrapositive (prove ¬Q → ¬P).
analogy: Like different paths to the same destination. Direct proof walks forward. Contradiction starts at the wrong place and shows it's impossible. Contrapositive takes the scenic route.
tiny_visual_key: three paths from assumptions to conclusions
example: Direct: To prove 'if n is even, n² is even', assume n=2k, then n²=4k²=2(2k²), which is even.
why_it_matters: Proofs verify correctness of algorithms and systems. Understanding proof techniques helps you construct and evaluate logical arguments.
checkpoint_question: When should you use proof by contradiction instead of direct proof?
expected_answer: When the conclusion is hard to prove directly but assuming its negation leads to an obvious impossibility. Common for proving something doesn't exist or is impossible.
common_mistake: Starting contradiction proofs incorrectly. You assume the negation of what you want to prove, not just any false statement.
key_insight: Contrapositive is often easier than direct. Instead of 'if P then Q', prove 'if not Q then not P' - sometimes clearer.

title: Mathematical Induction
explanation: Induction proves statements for all natural numbers. Base case: prove for n=0 (or 1). Inductive step: assume true for k, prove for k+1. This 'cascades' to all n.
analogy: Like dominoes falling. Prove the first falls (base case). Prove each domino knocks over the next (inductive step). All dominoes fall.
tiny_visual_key: dominoes: first pushed, each knocks next
example: Prove 1+2+...+n = n(n+1)/2. Base: n=1, 1=1(2)/2 ✓. Inductive: assume for k, show k+1: sum + (k+1) = k(k+1)/2 + (k+1) = (k+1)(k+2)/2 ✓
why_it_matters: Induction proves correctness of recursive algorithms, data structure properties, and any claim about 'all n'. It's the mathematical equivalent of recursion.
checkpoint_question: Why does strong induction assume the statement holds for ALL values up to k, not just k?
expected_answer: Some proofs need earlier values, not just the immediate predecessor. Strong induction provides access to P(1), P(2), ..., P(k) to prove P(k+1).
common_mistake: Proving the inductive step without using the inductive hypothesis. If you don't assume P(k), you're not doing induction.
key_insight: Induction mirrors recursion: base case = base case, inductive step = recursive case. Proving algorithms correct often uses induction.

title: Divisibility and Primes
explanation: a divides b (a|b) if b = ka for some integer k. Primes have exactly two divisors: 1 and themselves. Fundamental theorem: every integer > 1 has unique prime factorization.
analogy: Primes are like atoms. Every number is built from them in exactly one way. 12 = 2² × 3, and there's no other way to factor it into primes.
tiny_visual_key: number breaking into prime factor tree
why_it_matters: Number theory underlies cryptography. RSA encryption relies on the difficulty of factoring products of large primes.
checkpoint_question: Why is 1 not considered a prime number?
expected_answer: If 1 were prime, unique factorization would fail (12 = 1 × 2² × 3 = 1² × 2² × 3 = ...). Excluding 1 makes the fundamental theorem work cleanly.
common_mistake: Thinking primality is about 'only divisible by 1 and itself'. That's technically true but misses why: primes are multiplication atoms.
key_insight: There are infinitely many primes (Euclid's proof). But no formula generates them all - their distribution is deeply mysterious.

title: Modular Arithmetic
explanation: In modular arithmetic, numbers wrap around at a modulus. a ≡ b (mod n) means a and b have the same remainder when divided by n. Operations work naturally.
analogy: Like clock arithmetic. 10 + 5 = 15 = 3 o'clock (mod 12). After 12, you start counting from 1 again.
tiny_visual_key: number circle with modulus wrapping point
why_it_matters: Modular arithmetic is the foundation of hashing, cryptography, and error-correcting codes. Many algorithms work 'mod prime'.
checkpoint_question: Why does (a × b) mod n = ((a mod n) × (b mod n)) mod n?
expected_answer: Remainders multiply the same way as full numbers for modular results. This lets us reduce large intermediate values, keeping numbers manageable.
common_mistake: Assuming subtraction and division work simply. a - b mod n needs care when a < b. Division requires modular inverse, which doesn't always exist.
key_insight: Modular exponentiation uses repeated squaring: a^b mod n computed efficiently without huge intermediate values. Essential for RSA.

title: Euclidean Algorithm
explanation: The Euclidean algorithm finds gcd(a,b) by repeatedly replacing the larger number with the remainder: gcd(a,b) = gcd(b, a mod b) until reaching gcd(x, 0) = x.
analogy: Like fitting tiles. To find the largest square tile that fits both dimensions, repeatedly subtract the smaller from larger until they match.
tiny_visual_key: descending pairs converging to GCD
why_it_matters: GCD is used in simplifying fractions, cryptography (finding modular inverses), and algorithm analysis. Extended Euclidean solves ax + by = gcd(a,b).
checkpoint_question: Why does gcd(a,b) = gcd(b, a mod b)?
expected_answer: Any common divisor of a and b also divides (a mod b) = a - q×b. And any common divisor of b and (a mod b) divides a = q×b + (a mod b). Same divisors, same gcd.
common_mistake: Not recognizing when to stop. gcd(a, 0) = a. When the remainder is 0, the other number is the GCD.
key_insight: Extended Euclidean finds x, y such that ax + by = gcd(a,b). This is how you find modular inverses for cryptography.

title: Solving Recurrences
explanation: Recurrences define sequences in terms of earlier terms: T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n). Solutions give closed-form or asymptotic expressions.
analogy: Like compound interest but for algorithms. Each level of recursion multiplies and adds to the previous. Solving tells you the final growth.
tiny_visual_key: recurrence tree or telescoping levels
example: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n (merge sort). Solution: T(n) = Θ(n log n). T(n) = T(n-1) + 1 gives T(n) = n.
why_it_matters: Algorithm analysis often produces recurrences. Solving them gives time complexity. Most recursive algorithms need recurrence analysis.
checkpoint_question: What three cases does the Master Theorem cover?
expected_answer: For T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n): 1) f(n) grows slower than n^(log_b a) → Θ(n^(log_b a)). 2) They grow the same → Θ(n^(log_b a) log n). 3) f(n) grows faster → Θ(f(n)).
common_mistake: Applying Master Theorem when it doesn't apply (e.g., T(n) = T(n-1) + ...). Master Theorem requires division by b, not subtraction.
key_insight: Compare recursion work (a^depth × base case) vs combine work (f(n) summed). Whichever dominates determines complexity.

title: Vectors and Matrices
explanation: Vectors are ordered lists of numbers representing points or directions. Matrices are 2D arrays that transform vectors. Matrix multiplication applies transformations.
analogy: Vectors are arrows from origin. Matrices are transformation machines: put a vector in, get a transformed vector out. Rotation, scaling, shearing are all matrices.
tiny_visual_key: vector as arrow, matrix transforming grid of points
example: Rotation by θ: [[cos θ, -sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]]. Matrix × vector transforms the vector.
why_it_matters: Linear algebra is essential for graphics, ML, data science, and physics simulations. Neural networks are matrix multiplications.
checkpoint_question: Why is matrix multiplication not commutative (AB ≠ BA)?
expected_answer: A transforms B's input space, B transforms A's output space. The order determines which space is transformed by which matrix. Different orders, different results.
common_mistake: Multiplying matrices element-wise like adding. Matrix multiplication uses dot products of rows and columns, not element-wise products.
key_insight: Matrix multiplication applies transformations in sequence. A(Bx) = (AB)x. Compose transformations by multiplying their matrices.

title: Linear Independence and Span
explanation: Vectors are linearly independent if none can be written as a combination of others. The span is all vectors reachable by combining the given vectors.
analogy: Independent vectors point in truly different directions. Dependent vectors are redundant - you could remove one without losing reachable points.
tiny_visual_key: independent vectors spanning plane vs dependent staying on line
example: [1,0] and [0,1] are independent, span R². [1,0] and [2,0] are dependent (one is 2× the other), span only a line.
why_it_matters: Independence determines if a system has a unique solution. Dimension counting relies on finding independent basis vectors.
checkpoint_question: What's the maximum number of linearly independent vectors in R³?
expected_answer: Three. More than 3 vectors in 3D space must be dependent - there are only 3 independent directions. This number is the dimension.
common_mistake: Thinking orthogonal = independent. Orthogonality implies independence, but non-orthogonal vectors can still be independent.
key_insight: Basis vectors are a minimal independent spanning set. They uniquely represent any vector in the space as a linear combination.

title: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
explanation: An eigenvector v of matrix A satisfies Av = λv for scalar eigenvalue λ. The matrix only scales the eigenvector, doesn't change its direction.
analogy: Like finding the axis of a spin. Most vectors get rotated, but eigenvectors only stretch/shrink. They're the 'natural directions' of the transformation.
tiny_visual_key: eigenvector staying on line while scaled
example: For [[2,1],[0,3]], eigenvectors are [1,0] (λ=2) and [1,1] (λ=3). These directions just scale, don't rotate.
why_it_matters: Eigenvalues reveal matrix behavior: stability (|λ|<1), growth rates, principal components in data, and quantum mechanics fundamentals.
checkpoint_question: Why does det(A - λI) = 0 give eigenvalues?
expected_answer: Av = λv means (A - λI)v = 0. For non-zero v, (A - λI) must be singular (non-invertible), so its determinant must be zero.
common_mistake: Assuming all matrices have n distinct eigenvectors. Defective matrices have fewer independent eigenvectors than their dimension.
key_insight: Diagonalizable matrices decompose as A = PDP⁻¹ where D is diagonal eigenvalues. This makes computing Aⁿ trivial: Aⁿ = PDⁿP⁻¹.

title: Derivatives
explanation: The derivative measures rate of change. f'(x) gives the slope of f at x. For optimization, extrema occur where f'(x) = 0 (critical points).
analogy: Like speedometer reading. Position is f(t), velocity is f'(t), acceleration is f''(t). The derivative tells you how fast the function changes.
tiny_visual_key: curve with tangent line at point, slope indicated
example: f(x) = x². f'(x) = 2x. At x=3, slope is 6. Minimum at x=0 where f'(0)=0.
why_it_matters: Gradient descent uses derivatives to find minima of loss functions. Every neural network trains using derivatives (backpropagation).
checkpoint_question: Why is the second derivative useful for determining max vs min?
expected_answer: f''(x) > 0 at critical point means concave up (minimum). f''(x) < 0 means concave down (maximum). Second derivative tells you the curvature direction.
common_mistake: Assuming f'(x) = 0 means minimum. It could be maximum, or inflection point. Check second derivative or nearby values.
key_insight: Chain rule: d/dx[f(g(x))] = f'(g(x))·g'(x). This is backpropagation - derivatives flow backward through composed functions.

title: Gradients and Optimization
explanation: For multivariate functions, the gradient ∇f is a vector of partial derivatives. It points in the direction of steepest increase. Gradient descent follows -∇f to find minima.
analogy: Like finding the lowest point in a hilly landscape. The gradient points uphill. Walk opposite to the gradient (downhill) to reach a valley.
tiny_visual_key: 3D surface with gradient arrows pointing uphill
example: f(x,y) = x² + y². ∇f = [2x, 2y]. At (1,1), gradient is [2,2] - steepest ascent toward (∞,∞). Walk opposite to descend.
why_it_matters: Gradient descent optimizes ML models with millions of parameters. Understanding gradients is essential for deep learning.
checkpoint_question: Why might gradient descent find a local minimum instead of global minimum?
expected_answer: Gradient descent follows local slope. If it reaches a valley (local min), the gradient is zero and it stops. Non-convex functions have multiple local minima.
common_mistake: Using too large a learning rate causes oscillation or divergence. Too small is slow. Learning rate tuning is crucial.
code:
# Gradient descent update
for _ in range(iterations):
    gradient = compute_gradient(params)
    params = params - learning_rate * gradient
key_insight: Stochastic gradient descent uses random samples for gradient estimates. Noisier but much faster for large datasets.

title: Summations and Series
explanation: Summations add sequences: Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ i = n(n+1)/2. Geometric series: Σ rⁱ = (1-rⁿ)/(1-r). Series analysis gives closed forms for algorithm loop counts.
analogy: Like totaling receipts. Instead of adding one by one, find a formula. Knowing Σ1..n = n(n+1)/2 is like knowing the total without adding each number.
tiny_visual_key: stacking blocks in arithmetic or geometric pattern
example: 1+2+...+n = n(n+1)/2. 1+2+4+...+2ⁿ = 2ⁿ⁺¹-1. These appear constantly in algorithm analysis.
why_it_matters: Loop analysis requires summing iterations. Knowing common sums lets you recognize O(n²), O(n log n), etc. patterns immediately.
checkpoint_question: Why does Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ i = O(n²)?
expected_answer: n(n+1)/2 = n²/2 + n/2. The dominant term is n²/2. Dropping constants, Σi from 1 to n is O(n²). Nested loops from 1 to n give quadratic time.
common_mistake: Forgetting that harmonic series Σ1/i diverges (slowly - O(log n) partial sums). It appears in expected values and amortized analysis.
key_insight: Know these: Σ1 = n, Σi = n²/2, Σi² = n³/3, Σ2ⁱ = 2ⁿ, Σ1/i = ln(n). They cover most algorithm analysis cases.

title: Entropy
explanation: Entropy H(X) measures uncertainty in a random variable. H(X) = -Σ p(x) log₂ p(x). High entropy = unpredictable. Low entropy = predictable.
analogy: Like a surprise factor. A fair coin has high entropy (1 bit) - you can't guess. A biased 99% coin has low entropy - almost always heads, little surprise.
tiny_visual_key: even vs skewed probability distributions with entropy values
example: Fair coin: H = -2(0.5 log₂ 0.5) = 1 bit. Biased 90/10 coin: H ≈ 0.47 bits. Less uncertainty needs fewer bits to encode.
why_it_matters: Entropy bounds compression limits. You can't compress below entropy. It also measures information gain in decision trees.
checkpoint_question: Why is entropy maximized when all outcomes are equally likely?
expected_answer: Equal probabilities mean maximum uncertainty - you can't predict which outcome. Any bias toward one outcome reduces uncertainty, lowering entropy.
common_mistake: Thinking more outcomes always means more entropy. Entropy depends on probabilities. 100 outcomes with 99% on one has low entropy.
key_insight: Entropy measures the average number of bits needed to encode an outcome. Compression algorithms try to approach this theoretical limit.

title: Information Gain
explanation: Information gain measures how much entropy decreases when we learn something. It's parent entropy minus weighted child entropies. Used in decision tree splits.
analogy: Like asking 20 questions. A good question splits possibilities evenly, maximizing information gain. 'Is it alive?' is better than 'Is it a blue whale?'
tiny_visual_key: entropy bar shrinking after split into subsets
example: Before split: 50% yes, 50% no → H=1. After split: two groups of 100% yes, 100% no → H=0. Gain = 1 bit.
why_it_matters: Decision trees choose splits by maximum information gain. It's how ID3 and C4.5 algorithms work. Feature selection uses similar ideas.
checkpoint_question: Why weight child entropies by group size when calculating information gain?
expected_answer: Larger groups contribute more to overall uncertainty. A pure tiny group matters less than a mixed large group. Weighting reflects their impact on total entropy.
common_mistake: Comparing information gain across different parent sets. Gain depends on parent entropy - only compare gains for the same split decision.
key_insight: Information gain = H(parent) - Σ(size_i/total)×H(child_i). Maximize this to choose the best split.

title: Big-O and Growth Rates
explanation: Big-O describes upper bounds on growth. f(n) = O(g(n)) means f grows at most as fast as g. It ignores constants and lower-order terms, focusing on scaling behavior.
analogy: Like speed limits. O(n²) means 'at most quadratic' - you might be faster (O(n)) but never slower. It describes the ceiling on growth.
tiny_visual_key: curves with O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ)
example: 3n² + 100n + 1000 = O(n²). The n² dominates as n grows large. Binary search is O(log n), merge sort is O(n log n).
why_it_matters: Big-O lets you compare algorithm efficiency regardless of machine speed or implementation details. It predicts how algorithms scale.
checkpoint_question: Why do we drop constants in Big-O notation?
expected_answer: Constants don't affect growth rate. 2n and 1000n both grow linearly - they differ by a constant factor, not asymptotic behavior. Big-O describes scaling, not speed.
common_mistake: Thinking O(n) is always faster than O(n²). For small n, a O(n²) algorithm with small constants might beat O(n) with huge constants. Asymptotics describe large n.
key_insight: Know the hierarchy: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ) < O(n!). Polynomial time is 'efficient'; exponential is usually intractable.
